newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Central Eastern European bourses bearish.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Central Eastern European bourses bearish.

text.p: Bourses in Central and Eastern Europe fell sharply this week despite positive corporate earnings reports and stock market gains elsewhere in Europe after the U.S. left its short-term interest rates unchanged.
The Central European Share (CESI) index which reflects the price movements of 73 Czech, Polish, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, fell 2.44 percent.
BUDAPEST

Hungarian share prices were slack this week as two days of falls were followed by two days of rises and another fall on Friday. The BUX index declined 44.19 points to finish at 3,562.09 points on Friday.
The January-September corporate results failed to boost the market and traders said the market had run out of steam.
WARSAW

The Warsaw bourse fell this week and analysts said it was likely to extend its loss or stay flat next week, lacking capital currently being sucked by new issues on the primary market and with no new positive signals to spur growth.
Analysts said monthly earnings reports for October, most of them due on Monday and expected to prove good, were likely to spur a brief rebound at the beginning of the week.
But they said the market could later swing in a horizontal trend between 12,900 and 14,000 points of the WIG index or fall to about 11,5000 points.

They said the primary market, with companies queueing at the Polish Securities Commission to clear their shares for trade, was drawing capital from the bourse as some issues, such as rubber producer Stomil Sanok, were very attractive.
PRAGUE
Czech shares slid sharply in the first four days of the week with the closely watched PX50 index falling nearly four percent before a rebound on Friday.
Dealers and analysts were virtually unanimous in attributing the decline to structural problems on the Czech capital markets rather than to company fundamentals.
BRATISLAVA

The Slovak Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) saw another week of dull trading with insignificant activity of foreign players, and brokers predicted no reversal of the bourse's long-term downward trend over the next few weeks.
The 12-share index edged up 0.79 points to 190.63 on Friday, from the Monday's open at 189.84, after slight increases to above the 190 point level on Monday and Tuesday.
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks rebounded in buoyant trade on Friday, closing the week higher, and traders said no spectacular changes should shake the market in the near future and the stable trend was likely to last.
Investors were seen as flocking back as the government, in a drive against fraud, attempted to dispel fears saying no bona fide share purchases would be challenged.
Share prices plumetted two weeks ago when privatisation officials said they would annul some 9,000 employee buyout contracts, driving away foreign buyers.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares fell 3.96 percent after the unofficial results of Sunday's general election showed the ruling Liberal Democrats may have to relinquish power to the right-wing "Spring" alliance.
The SBI index closed at 1,175.4 on Friday, down 48.48.
BUCHAREST
Light investor interest kept turnover thin at 54.6 million lei ($15,730) on Tuesday and sent it even lower to 31.2 million on Thursday, when low demand met with even lower supply.
Azomures SA took the bulk of trade on both days.
Seven stocks inched up, sending unofficial indices VAB and BIG on Thursday each up 0.7 percent from the previous session.
SOFIA

Floor trading was suspended on October 23 by the trading regulatory body after public share companies failed to meet new legal requirements by the September 19 deadline. Since then only sporadic repo deals in government securities were struck.
